title: Query and passage asymmetry, the silent bug
summary: Models handle the query/passage difference with separate encoders or a text prefix, and getting the prefix wrong fails without any error. I measured the cost on a 40 query benchmark and got 5 points of recall@1, with a confidence interval that crosses zero.
html:
A query and a passage are not the same kind of text. "why does an SSD reserve capacity the host cannot see?" is eight words, interrogative, and incomplete on purpose. The passage answering it is declarative, longer, and states the fact rather than asking for it.

Day 11 trained one encoder to map both into one space. That is a slightly odd thing to ask of a single function, and how models handle it is today's topic. So is a claim about it that I went and measured, with a result I did not expect.

Two ways to handle the asymmetry

Two encoders. DPR used separate networks with separate weights, one for queries and one for passages, trained jointly. Clean, and it doubles your parameters, your memory and the number of things that can drift apart.

One encoder plus a prefix. Prepend a short marker telling the model which side it is encoding:

E5:      "query: how do bees make honey?"
         "passage: fresh nectar is about eighty percent water..."

BGE:     "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ..."
         (query side only, passages go in bare)

Nomic:   "search_query: ..."  /  "search_document: ..."

This won on practical grounds. Half the parameters, one representation space that cannot drift, and the prefix generalises into full task instructions if you want them. The marker is ordinary text going through the ordinary tokenizer. The model learned during training that text after query: behaves differently from text after passage:.

Why the bug is silent

Forget the prefix and nothing fails. The model embeds whatever you hand it and returns a perfectly well formed vector. It is text, and all text is valid input.

Same for the other variants: the query prefix on your passages, both sides tagged the same, or a prefix from a different model family. Every one of those produces vectors, and vectors produce rankings, and rankings look like results. That is the shape of the failure, and it is the same shape as the normalisation mismatch on Day 5 and the pooling mismatch on Day 10.

So I measured it

The usual claim is that this is one of the most common silent quality bugs in RAG. I wanted a number, so I built a benchmark.

The first one was wrong, and how it was wrong is worth a paragraph. I used 20 passages spread across bees, TCP, espresso, RAID and physics, with 12 queries. Under that setup, omitting the prefixes beat using them correctly by 8.3 points. Which is nonsense, and the reason is obvious in hindsight: when your passages are about wildly different subjects, matching a query to the right one is nearly free. Any representation gets it. The task had no headroom to detect anything, so what I was measuring was which way the noise fell.

An evaluation that everything passes is not an evaluation. So I rebuilt it harder: 40 passages and 40 queries, all in one domain (storage and distributed systems), deliberately confusable so the model has to make fine distinctions rather than topic level ones. Same task, four prefix conventions, on e5-small-v2, which was trained with prefixes:

condition                         recall@1   recall@5      MRR
correct  (query: / passage:)         0.875      1.000    0.920
no prefixes at all                   0.825      1.000    0.894
swapped  (passage: / query:)         0.850      1.000    0.917
same prefix on both                  0.875      1.000    0.923

Correct prefixes win on recall@1 by 5 points over using none. The direction matches the folklore. The magnitude does not: this is a 5 point difference, not a collapse.

And then the part that matters more than the table.

Checking whether I actually measured anything

With 40 queries, one query changing whether it ranks first moves recall@1 by 2.5 points. So a 5 point gap is two queries. Two.

Bootstrapping the per-query differences, 20,000 resamples:

observed recall@1 difference:  +5.0 points  (2 net queries)
95% confidence interval:       [-5.0, +15.0] points
samples favouring correct:     78.2%

The interval crosses zero. My experiment is consistent with correct prefixes helping by 15 points, and equally consistent with them hurting by 5. It does not establish the effect. It leans toward it at about 78 percent confidence, which is not a standard anyone should ship on.

For contrast, the same four conditions on all-MiniLM-L6-v2, which was trained without prefixes, produced differences of +5.0, +5.0 and +7.5 points in the other direction. Adding meaningless markers appeared to improve it. That is noise, and seeing noise of the same magnitude as my headline result is the clearest possible evidence about what 40 queries can resolve.

What to conclude

Use the prefix the model documents. Not because skipping it is catastrophic, but because it is one line, it costs nothing, and the direction of the evidence is right. Check modules.json, the model card, or the example usage, and write it next to your pooling and normalisation notes.

Be sceptical of the claim's size, including from me. I could not demonstrate it on a clean in-domain task. That does not mean it is small everywhere. Published results are on harder and more out-of-domain benchmarks than mine, and instruction-tuned models with full natural language prompts plausibly depend on them far more than a two word marker does. My measurement covers one small model on one small task, and I am reporting what it showed rather than what I expected.

The useful finding today is not about prefixes. It is that 40 queries cannot resolve a 5 point difference, and almost every informal RAG evaluation you will ever see is smaller than 40 queries.

That is the real lesson, arriving early. When someone tells you a change improved their system, the first question is how many queries they measured on, and the second is whether the difference survives a confidence interval. Most of the time nobody has computed one.

Phase 1 ends tomorrow, and it ends by doing this properly: building a baseline and measuring it, so that everything from Day 15 onward has a number to move rather than an opinion to argue with.
exercise:
1. Find your model's convention. Pick the embedding model you would actually use. Open its model card and its modules.json, find whether it expects a query prefix, a passage prefix, both, or neither, and write the exact strings down next to the pooling mode and normalisation setting from Days 5 and 10. That is now a three line configuration note that silently governs your retrieval quality.

2. Compute your own noise floor. However many test questions you have, work out how many percentage points of recall@1 one query is worth. If you have 20 questions, it is 5 points. Any improvement smaller than two or three times that is not something your test set can see, and knowing the number stops you chasing it.

3. Reproduce the bootstrap. Take any two lists of per-query scores, even made up ones. Resample 40 values with replacement 20,000 times, take the mean difference each time, and report the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Twelve lines. This is the single most useful thing in Phase 4 and you can have it working before Day 14 starts.
